instruction: Print the third whitespace-separated column of a file.
context: awk splits each line on runs of whitespace by default, numbering fields from $1, where $0 is the whole line. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored, unlike cut which counts every delimiter.

instruction: Print the final column when the number of columns varies per line.
context: awk: NF holds the field count for the current line, so $NF is the last field and $(NF-1) the one before it. This is the standard fix for input with a ragged column count.

instruction: Extract the login shell column from /etc/passwd.
context: awk -F sets the input field separator, which may be a single character or a regular expression. A comma between print arguments emits OFS, a single space, where juxtaposition concatenates them.

instruction: Total a column of numbers.
context: awk: an uninitialized variable is zero in numeric context, so no setup is needed. The END block runs once after the last line, which is where the accumulated result is printed.

instruction: Compute the mean of a numeric column.
context: awk: NR is the running record number, so in the END block it equals the total line count. Guard against empty input, because dividing by a zero NR yields an error rather than zero.

instruction: Show only the rows where a numeric column exceeds a threshold.
context: awk: a bare expression before the block is the pattern, and the block runs only when it is true. Comparison against a numeric literal forces numeric context, so string ordering does not apply.

instruction: Count occurrences grouped by the value of a column.
response: awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (key in count) print count[key], key}' access.log
context: awk arrays are associative and spring into existence on first use, which makes this a one-pass group-by. Iteration order from for-in is unspecified, so pipe to sort for a stable result.

instruction: Print the lines between two markers in a file.
context: awk: two patterns separated by a comma form a range that turns on at the first match and off at the second, inclusive of both. It re-arms, so multiple blocks in one file all print.

instruction: Process a CSV while skipping its header row.
context: awk: NR is the record number, so NR > 1 skips the first line. Use FNR instead when several files are passed, because FNR resets per file while NR keeps counting.

instruction: Remove duplicate lines without sorting the file first.
context: awk: the expression is the whole program, and a true value prints the line. The post-increment makes it true only the first time each line appears, which preserves original order where sort -u does not.

instruction: Convert a tab-separated file to comma-separated.
context: awk: assigning to a field, even its own value, forces the record to be rebuilt using OFS. Without that no-op assignment, $0 prints unchanged and OFS has no visible effect.

instruction: Print a numeric column rounded to two decimal places in aligned columns.
context: awk printf takes C-style formats and emits no newline of its own. The minus flag left-aligns, the number before the decimal is the field width, and %8.2f fixes the precision.

instruction: Replace only the second occurrence on each line.
context: sed: a trailing number replaces only that occurrence, while g replaces all and the default replaces the first. Combining as 2g replaces from the second onward.

instruction: Strip comment and blank lines from a config file.
context: sed: the d command deletes matching lines and starts the next cycle. -E enables extended regular expressions so grouping needs no backslashes, and POSIX classes keep it portable.

instruction: Print lines 100 through 120 of a large file.
context: sed: -n suppresses the automatic print so only p output appears. Appending a q after the range, as in 120q, stops reading early and matters on very large files.

instruction: Insert a line immediately after a matching line.
context: sed: a appends after the matched line, i inserts before it, and c replaces it. GNU sed accepts the text on the same line; BSD sed requires a backslash and a newline first.

instruction: Swap two colon-separated fields on every line.
context: sed: parentheses capture in -E mode and backreferences are \1 upward in the replacement. An ampersand in the replacement stands for the entire match and must be escaped to be literal.

instruction: Rewrite a filesystem path without escaping every slash.
context: sed: the character right after s is the delimiter, so any unused character works. Using a pipe or comma for path substitutions avoids the leaning-toothpick problem entirely.

instruction: Remove trailing whitespace from every line of a file.
context: sed: the POSIX class inside brackets matches spaces and tabs portably, where \s is a GNU extension. Anchoring with $ confines the deletion to the end of the line.

instruction: Extract every IP address from a log rather than the whole line.
context: grep: -o prints just the matched substring, once per match, so a line with two matches yields two output lines. -E enables extended syntax so + and grouping need no backslashes.

instruction: Search for a literal string containing dots and brackets.
context: grep -F treats the pattern as a literal string, disabling all metacharacters, which is both correct and faster for fixed text. It is also the safe choice for a pattern coming from a variable.

instruction: Find a variable name without matching longer names containing it.
context: grep -w requires the match to be bounded by non-word characters, so count does not match counter or account. -x demands the whole line match instead.

instruction: Show a stack trace by printing lines after each error.
context: grep: -A prints lines after the match, -B before, and -C both. Non-adjacent groups are separated by a -- line, which is worth knowing before piping the output onward.

instruction: Filter out several noisy patterns at once.
context: grep: -v inverts the match and -E lets alternation combine several patterns in one pass. Repeating -e is the alternative and avoids regex metacharacter surprises.

instruction: List which files contain a string, without printing the matches.
context: grep: lowercase -l prints each filename once and stops reading that file early. Capital -L inverts it and lists the files with no match, which is how to find code missing a required header.

instruction: Count how many lines match in each file of a directory.
context: grep -c counts matching lines, not total matches, so two hits on one line count once. Combine with -o and wc -l when the true occurrence count is needed.

instruction: Search a file with no trailing newline or with binary content safely.
context: grep: -a treats a binary file as text instead of printing the binary file matches placeholder. --binary-files=without-match skips such files entirely during a recursive search.

instruction: Take the first and third comma-separated fields.
context: cut: -d sets a single-character delimiter and -f selects fields, accepting lists and ranges like 1,3 or 2-. It cannot reorder fields, and treats every delimiter as significant, unlike awk.

instruction: Take a fixed-width column from a report by character position.
context: cut: -c selects character positions where -f selects delimited fields, and -b selects bytes, which differ for multibyte text. Ranges are inclusive and one-based.

instruction: Drop the second column and keep everything else.
context: cut: --complement inverts the selection, which is far easier than enumerating the fields to keep when the count is large. It is a GNU extension and absent from BSD cut.

instruction: Sort a report numerically by its second column, largest first.
context: sort: -k2,2 confines the key to field two, where a bare -k2 would extend to the end of the line. Attaching n and r to the key applies numeric and reverse ordering to that key only.

instruction: Deduplicate lines and report how many were dropped.
context: sort -u removes duplicates during the sort, which is cheaper than piping to uniq because uniq only collapses adjacent lines. -u compares by the sort keys, so a restricted -k makes it deduplicate on that key alone.

instruction: Sort by one column while preserving the existing order of ties.
context: sort: -s disables the last-resort whole-line comparison that otherwise breaks ties, making the sort stable. This is what allows a chain of sorts to build a multi-level ordering.

instruction: Order release tags so 1.10 comes after 1.9.
context: sort -V compares embedded numbers numerically segment by segment, which is what version strings need. Plain lexical sort puts 1.10 before 1.9, and -n stops at the first dot.

instruction: Sort names alphabetically regardless of capitalization.
context: sort: -f folds case for comparison, and -d considers only alphanumerics and blanks. Note the locale governs collation, so LC_ALL=C gives byte order and different grouping.

instruction: Report how many times each distinct line occurs.
context: uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so the input must be sorted first or counts fragment. -c prefixes the count, -d shows only repeated lines, and -u shows only unique ones.

instruction: Deduplicate log lines while ignoring the leading timestamp field.
context: uniq: -f skips that many leading fields before comparing and -s skips characters. The skipped part is still printed, so the first occurrence keeps its original timestamp.

instruction: Strip carriage returns from a file with Windows line endings.
context: tr: -d deletes every listed character, and it only reads standard input so a redirect or pipe is required. -s squeezes runs of a character into one instead.

instruction: Convert text to lowercase.
context: tr maps the first set onto the second position by position, and POSIX character classes keep it correct outside ASCII-only input. A-Z ranges depend on the locale's collation order.

instruction: Remove every character that is not a digit.
context: tr: -c complements the first set, so combined with -d it deletes everything not listed. Adding -s as well collapses runs, which is how word-frequency pipelines tokenize input.

instruction: Print everything except the last five lines of a file.
context: head: a negative count prints all but that many trailing lines, a GNU extension absent from BSD head. The mirror is tail -n +N, which starts output at line N.

instruction: Skip a CSV header and stream the rest.
context: tail: a plus sign means start at that line number rather than count from the end, so +2 skips exactly one header line. Without the plus, -n 2 prints the last two lines.

instruction: Count lines across many files and get a total.
context: wc: -l counts newlines, so a final line without one is not counted. -w counts words, -c bytes, and -m characters, which differ for multibyte encodings.

instruction: Collapse a list of lines into one comma-separated line.
context: paste: -s serializes one file onto a single line instead of merging files side by side, and -d sets the separator. Multiple -d characters are used cyclically.

instruction: Merge two files on a shared key column.
context: join requires both inputs sorted on the join field, otherwise it silently drops rows. -1 and -2 pick the key column in each file and -a 1 keeps unmatched left rows as an outer join.

instruction: Compare two config files in the format patch understands.
context: diff -u produces unified context, the format git and patch consume. -w ignores whitespace differences and -r recurses when the arguments are directories.

instruction: View two files in parallel columns showing only the differences.
context: diff: -y prints side by side and --suppress-common-lines hides matching rows so only changes remain. -W sets the total display width when the default 130 columns wraps.

instruction: List entries present in both of two sorted files.
context: comm emits three columns: unique to file one, unique to file two, and common. The digits suppress columns, so -12 hides the first two and leaves only the shared lines. Both files must be sorted.

instruction: Align ragged delimited output into readable columns.
context: column: -t builds a table by inferring column widths and -s sets the input delimiter. Consecutive delimiters are collapsed unless -n is given, which matters for empty CSV fields.

instruction: Wrap long lines at eighty columns without splitting words.
context: fold: -w sets the width and -s breaks at the last blank before it rather than mid-word. fmt reflows paragraphs instead, joining short lines as well as splitting long ones.

instruction: Number only the non-empty lines of a file.
context: nl: -b t numbers only non-empty lines, where -b a numbers every line like cat -n. -w sets the number width and -s the separator after it.

instruction: Break a huge file into chunks of ten thousand lines each.
context: split: -l splits on line count where -b splits on bytes and -n on a chunk count. -d uses numeric suffixes instead of the default aa, ab sequence.

instruction: Convert a legacy file to UTF-8.
context: iconv: -f is the source encoding and -t the target, and it fails on the first byte it cannot map. Appending //TRANSLIT to the target substitutes near equivalents and //IGNORE drops them.

instruction: Convert tabs to spaces at a four-column tab stop.
context: expand converts tabs to spaces and unexpand reverses it, with -t setting the stop width. unexpand only converts leading whitespace unless -a is given.

instruction: Use a capture group in a substitution on macOS.
context: BSD sed supports -E for extended regular expressions just as GNU sed does, so capture groups port cleanly. What differs is -i, which on BSD requires a separate suffix argument.

instruction: Align delimited output into columns on macOS.
context: BSD column supports -t and -s but lacks the GNU -o output-separator and --table-columns options. For anything beyond simple alignment, awk printf is the portable choice.

instruction: Print all but the last five lines on macOS, where head -n -5 is unavailable.
context: BSD head rejects a negative line count, so the GNU head -n -5 idiom fails on macOS. This sed pattern keeps a five-line window in the hold area and prints only what falls out of it.
